contentBody: **When is an early prototype good enough to test?**
option.1: When friends clap because the template looks expensive
option.2: When a new person can understand the offer, see a next step, and react
option.3: When every extra feature, including payments, is already live
option.4: When the logo colour has been debated for several days
answerExplanation: Good enough is about understanding and action, not decoration. A working next step and a way to write down a reaction matter more than polish.

contentBody: **How does a testable prototype differ from a polished one?**
option.1: Testable means using as many animations as the builder allows
option.2: Polished means nobody has seen it, so it must already be correct
option.3: Testable means it looks finished even if the form does not open
option.4: Testable is clear and ready to show; extra decoration can wait
answerExplanation: Polish is extra visual or feature work that does not change first learning. Testable means a stranger can get the offer and you can record a reaction.

contentBody: **Why is putting a login wall on a first prototype a poor move?**
option.1: People then struggle with signup, not with whether they get the offer
option.2: Login is the only way a stranger can read a headline on the page
option.3: Every waitlist is invalid unless it starts with a one-time password
option.4: Website builders refuse to publish any page that has no login
answerExplanation: Login blocks the test. You learn about account friction instead of whether the offer is understood. A first page should be readable without an account.

contentBody: **When should you write the questions and counts you want from viewers?**
option.1: After the first ten compliments, so the plan can match the praise
option.2: Only after you have already changed the product twice
option.3: Before anyone sees the page, so you do not collect empty praise
option.4: Never; a beautiful theme replaces the need to write anything down
answerExplanation: Planned feedback is decided in advance. If you share first and decide later, you mainly collect compliments. Write the questions before anyone sees the page.

contentBody: **Which planned question is weakest for a first look at a page?**
option.1: What do you think this product does?
option.2: What extra modules should we add and raise money for?
option.3: Would you use this in a normal week — yes, maybe, or no?
option.4: What was confusing on the first screen?
answerExplanation: Understanding, desire, and confusion are the useful layers. Leading with a feature-and-funding wishlist produces a shopping list and loses the plot.
